To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

stereotype-consistent and inconsistent social information differentially serve two functions of communication-sharing social information and regulating relationships-and that the stereotype consistency bias occurs when information seen to serve the social connection function is more likely communicated than information seen to serve other communication functions.

stereotype-consistent and inconsistent messages are perceived as serving different functions in communication, and when the social connectivity function is more important than the information function, stereotype-consistent information tends to be communicated more often than stereotype-inconsistent messages.
(a) stereotype consistency is a situated functional bias in communication, and (b) this bias is moderated by the extent to which the stereotype is shared in the community.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how people communicate about social groups.
how stereotypes are used in communication, how they influence the content of messages, and the consequences of this for the social functions of communication.
the role of stereotypes in communication.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the study has shown how the stereotype consistency bias is affected by the social context in which it occurs.
stereotype consistent information is communicated because of its greater social connectivity value, which is particularly important when a stereotype is perceived to have high sharedness.
stereotype-consistency is a bias in communication that occurs when people are trying to connect with others in a social group.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

stereotype-consistency bias in communication is not just a function of people's desire to be consistent, or of their desire to maintain a positive self-image, but is instead a function of the social functions that stereotype-consistent and inconsistent communication can serve.
stereotype-consistent and inconsistent social information differentially serve two central functions of communication: sharing information and regulating relationships.
stereotypes are not just bad, but that they also have positive effects.
The main takeaway from our work is that
stereotypes are not always bad.
the way people talk about social groups is not just a reflection of their beliefs and attitudes, but also of their desire to be socially connected with others.
